subject: astronomy
topicDisplay: Early Models Of The Solar System
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: According to Newton, the gravitational force between two masses depends on distance how?
options: It increases with the square of the distance
It decreases with the square of the distance
questions.explain: Newton's law of gravitation is an inverse-square law: force falls off with the square of the distance.

questions.q: Galileo's observation of the phases of Venus provided evidence that:
questions.explain: The full set of Venus's phases can only occur if Venus orbits the Sun, supporting heliocentrism.

questions.q: What force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.explain: The Sun's gravitational pull provides the centripetal force that holds planets in orbit.

questions.q: Which planet is the most massive and has the strongest gravity of the eight planets?
questions.explain: Jupiter is the most massive planet, giving it the strongest surface gravity and a large family of moons.

questions.q: The four inner planets are described as terrestrial because they are:
questions.explain: Terrestrial planets such as Earth and Mars are small, dense and rocky.

questions.q: Which Greek philosopher's Earth-centred system, later refined by Ptolemy, dominated Western astronomy for over a thousand years?
questions.explain: Aristotle's Earth-centred cosmology, later formalised by Ptolemy, was accepted for over a millennium.

questions.q: Newton's work was significant for astronomy because it showed that:
options: The same law of gravity governs both falling objects on Earth and the orbits of planets
The Earth is at the centre of the universe
questions.explain: Newton unified terrestrial and celestial motion under a single universal law of gravitation.

questions.q: Retrograde motion is the apparent:
options: Backwards (westward) loop of a planet against the stars
questions.explain: Planets occasionally appear to move backwards against the stars; the heliocentric model explains this as an overtaking effect.

questions.q: The bright, glowing head of gas and dust surrounding the nucleus of a comet is called the:
questions.explain: As a comet nears the Sun its ices vaporise, forming a glowing coma around the solid nucleus.

questions.q: Telescopes such as the Hubble Space Telescope are placed in orbit so that they can:
options: Avoid the blurring and absorption caused by the Earth's atmosphere
questions.explain: Above the atmosphere there is no twinkling or absorption, giving space telescopes sharper, clearer images.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the planets outward from the Sun?
options: Venus, Mercury, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, Uranus
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
Mercury, Earth, Venus, Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, Neptune, Uranus
Mercury, Venus, Mars, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
questions.explain: From the Sun the order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

questions.q: The geocentric model of the universe placed which body at the centre?
questions.explain: In the geocentric (Ptolemaic) model the Earth was at the centre with everything orbiting it.

questions.q: According to Kepler's first law, the orbit of a planet around the Sun is:
options: An ellipse with the Sun at one focus
An ellipse with the Sun at the centre
questions.explain: Kepler's first law states orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus, not the centre.

questions.q: According to Kepler's third law, the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the:
options: Square of its distance from the Sun
Cube of its average distance from the Sun
questions.explain: Kepler's third law states the period squared is proportional to the semi-major axis cubed, so distant planets take much longer to orbit.

questions.q: A rock from space that survives its passage through the atmosphere and lands on the ground is called a:
questions.explain: A meteorite is the solid remnant that reaches the ground, whereas the streak of light in the sky is a meteor.

questions.q: A planet moves fastest in its orbit when it is:
options: At a constant point regardless of distance
questions.explain: By Kepler's second law a planet moves fastest at perihelion, its closest approach to the Sun.

questions.q: Which of these is classified as a dwarf planet rather than a planet?
questions.explain: Pluto is a dwarf planet because it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other objects.

questions.q: Copernicus delayed publishing his Sun-centred model until near his death mainly because:
options: He had not finished the calculations
He feared opposition from the Church and established scholars
He doubted his own idea entirely
He could not afford to print it
questions.explain: Copernicus held back his heliocentric work, published in 1543, largely from fear of controversy and criticism.

questions.q: The heliocentric model proposed by Copernicus placed which body at the centre?
questions.explain: Copernicus placed the Sun at the centre, with the planets including Earth orbiting it.

questions.q: The solar system is thought to have formed from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust according to the:
questions.explain: The nebular hypothesis says the Sun and planets formed from the gravitational collapse of a rotating cloud of gas and dust.

questions.q: Which planet has the most prominent and visible ring system?
questions.explain: Saturn is famous for its bright, broad ring system made largely of ice particles.

questions.q: The icy region far beyond Neptune thought to be the source of long-period comets is the:
questions.explain: The Oort cloud is a vast spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system, the source of long-period comets.
